name: Bianca Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal factory day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am twenty-seven and lead a ceramic tile kiln line. My two-year technical diploma taught me temperature control, but the work is in listening for a bad roller and rejecting a warped tile before a whole rack spoils. I use an AI assistant daily to compare firing curves and write a shift handover; I still check the actual tiles. My senior pay is above the usual operator rate, I have eight months of expenses saved, and plenty of other factories are nearby. I live with my partner, and we have no children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the apprentices that an AI handover saves writing, but a tile still has to lie flat on the gauge. The kiln makes ceramic tiles, not paragraphs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The senior wage and steady kiln shifts would continue in this picture. Eight months saved and plenty of nearby factory work give my partner and me a comfortable margin, though I still want to earn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep running kiln changeovers and use the AI curve comparison I already know. I would put a new amount from each senior pay packet into savings after our ordinary bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about work carrying on. I can use a small tool without confusing it with a machine that can fire a rack.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you reject a rack?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I measure the first tile’s bow and check its glaze under light. If the corner lifts off the gauge, the rack waits instead of being boxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep saving with eight months already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I want room for a home deposit, and a factory can close for reasons besides AI. I transfer new wages after the bills, rather than count the old balance twice.

I would **keep** teaching **apprentices** safe kiln checks.
think: My **senior wage** and eight-month reserve make this mild case manageable.
**Nearby** factories give us another route if ordinary work changes.
do: **Keep** running tile-kiln changeovers and gauging first tiles.
**Save** new money from each senior pay packet after bills.
S0.quote: The kiln makes ceramic tiles, not paragraphs.
fieldNote: **Bianca** uses **AI daily** for firing curves, then checks the ceramic tile itself.
**Higher** pay, eight months saved and plentiful nearby work support her calm and fresh saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AI may buy glaze materials and draw schedules faster, while the kiln crew still handles hot racks. I would try a new AI glaze-defect alert on paid time only if the factory provides a safe trial with real tiles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Management might shorten paid planning time, but my own higher wage and kiln shifts look sound for now. I worry an office target could push an apprentice to move a hot rack before a physical check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a paid, supervised trial of the new defect alert on cooled sample tiles and learn its controls if the slot is offered. I would also keep the manual gauge check and train the apprentices to stop a warped rack.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about production targets, though I do not expect to lose my wage in this slower change. I want proof from tiles before a screen earns trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test the alert?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare its mark with the bow gauge and the glaze seen under light on ten cooled samples. If it misses a bad tile, I would keep that rack out of packing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the trial is unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would decline the new trial and keep using the AI curve comparison I already know. My paid kiln shift comes before a company experiment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the kiln team that thinking AI reaches scheduling around 2028, when I am twenty-nine, and capable robots reach tile handling around 2031, when I am thirty-two. A robot could load racks and reject tiles faster than our crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect some kiln-handling shifts to disappear, and my higher wage could fall even with eight months saved. Nearby factories may also buy the same robots, so I cannot call them a guaranteed escape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the senior kiln shifts while asking for a fully funded, paid-time electrical maintenance course with safe kiln isolation. If a posted nearby maintenance job pays enough for our bills and its qualification is accepted, I would enrol, then apply after qualifying; if shifts are cut first, I would apply to posted nearby kiln-lead jobs at adequate pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a realistic wage cut, but I have time, savings and a specific qualification route. I am not betting our rent on a course brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrical maintenance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kiln drives, sensors and fans still need safe testing if robots move tiles. I need a maintenance qualification beyond my operator diploma before touching an isolated motor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the maintenance vacancy never appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep drawing the kiln wage and search posted nearby kiln-lead openings that pay our bills. I would not spend our reserve on an unoffered class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our crew thinking AI reaches scheduling in 2031 when I am thirty-two, with capable tile-handling robots around 2034 when I am thirty-five. Five years gives me time to qualify while I still draw a senior wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kiln may eventually need fewer loaders, but the extra years let us build savings. I still need an actual qualified job before I leave the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the lead shifts and add new money from each pay packet to our reserve. If a fully funded maintenance course gives paid study time and safe kiln-isolation practice, and a posted nearby qualified job pays our bills, I would enrol and then apply after qualifying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the longer-run shift count, yet my current wage is strong. A training place and a job posting are facts I can check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you set aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would agree a fixed transfer with my partner after bills each payday. We already have eight months; these transfers would be new money from wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What safety practice would the course need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need to lock kiln power, test a sensor fault on a stopped line and have a trainer check the restart. A lecture alone would not qualify me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI reaches scheduling in 2036 when I am thirty-seven and capable tile-handling robots around 2039 when I am forty. A decade is enough to build real skills without giving up a good kiln wage today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could still need decades of wages after forty. Eight months saved now helps, but the long horizon is useful only if I keep adding new money and check where maintenance jobs actually open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the kiln and save a new amount each payday. If the employer offers a paid safe slot, I would learn a new AI kiln-fault diagnosis control beyond today’s curve summaries; if a fully funded paid-time maintenance course and posted nearby adequate job are available, I would qualify and apply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about eventual robot handling, though I have time to build options. I would rather earn and learn than assume the market owes me a place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is different about the new AI control?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would suggest which fan or sensor is failing, not just draw a firing curve. I would test the suggestion on a stopped kiln with a qualified electrician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a distant job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would first apply to a posted nearby maintenance opening whose wage covers our bills. A distant offer must cover moving costs as well as pay before my partner and I would consider it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 case worries me most because robots could remove kiln-handling shifts around 2031 while I still need decades of wages. A funded paid maintenance course and a real nearby job at adequate pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the first tile after a robot loads a rack. I want apprentices to learn the gauge and the safe stop, even if a machine does the lifting. A warped ceramic tile can fill a box without anyone noticing.

headlineQuote: A warped ceramic tile can fill a box without anyone noticing.
portrait: **Bianca**, **27**, leads a ceramic tile kiln line and has a two-year technical diploma.
She **uses** **AI daily**, but checks tile bow and glaze before releasing racks.
Her **higher senior pay**, eight-month reserve and plentiful nearby factories give her room to plan.
She **values** **apprenticeships** and follows a funded paid maintenance route only when an actual adequate local job exists.
biggestWorry: **Fast** robots around **2031** could cut paid kiln-handling shifts while Bianca still needs many working years.
whatWouldHelp: A **fully funded paid-time** maintenance course and posted nearby bill-covering job would give her a practical route.
